title: Relationships and mental health
citation: Argyle, M. (2014). Benefits produced by supportive social relationships. In H. O. F. Veiel & U. Baumann (Eds.), The Meaning and Measurement of Social Support (pp. 13-32). Taylor & Francis.
content:
Relationships and mental health.

Our relationships play an important role in our mental health. Feeling understood, supported and connected can help us cope with stress and recover from difficult experiences, while ongoing conflict, criticism, or emotional distance can have the opposite effect. Relationships do not need to be perfect to be healthy, but the way people communicate, solve problems and support one another has a powerful influence on emotional wellbeing.

Isn't it selfish to prioritise my own mental health in a relationship?

Many people worry that looking after their own mental health means neglecting the people they care about. In reality, taking care of yourself is often what allows you to be more present, patient, and emotionally available for others. Setting healthy boundaries, getting enough rest, or asking for support is not selfish. It helps prevent stress and resentment from building up and can strengthen relationships over time.

Why do relationship problems affect my mood and sleep so much?

The brain experiences close relationships as an important source of safety and security. When there is ongoing conflict, uncertainty, or emotional distance, the body's stress response can remain activated. This can make it harder to relax, concentrate, or sleep, while increasing feelings of worry, irritability, or sadness. Because our brains are wired for connection, relationship stress often affects both emotional and physical wellbeing.

Healthy conflict vs harmful conflict: what's the difference?

Disagreements are a normal part of every close relationship. Healthy conflict involves listening, showing respect and working together to understand each other's perspectives, even when opinions differ. Harmful conflict is more likely to involve repeated criticism, contempt, hostility, avoidance, or feeling unsafe to express yourself. The goal of healthy conflict is not to avoid disagreement altogether, but to resolve it in ways that strengthen trust rather than damage it.

Why do the same arguments keep happening in my family?

Many recurring family arguments are not really about the topic being discussed. They often reflect deeper patterns that have developed over many years, such as misunderstandings, unmet emotional needs, different expectations, or established communication habits. When people respond in the same way each time, the same conflict tends to repeat itself. Recognising these patterns is often the first step towards changing them.

When should a relationship or family involve outside support?

Most relationships experience periods of tension, particularly during stressful life events or major changes. Seeking outside support can be helpful when communication repeatedly breaks down, conflicts remain unresolved, emotional distress is affecting daily life, or family members feel stuck in the same patterns despite their efforts to improve things. Support from a qualified mental health professional can provide practical strategies to improve communication, strengthen relationships and help families navigate challenges together.
